title: State Management in LangGraph
description: Designing state schemas, how reducers control the way updates combine, shared versus per-node data, and the common message-list state pattern.

lessons.title: Defining a State Schema
lessons.description: Explicit, typed state is what makes a LangGraph graph inspectable — deciding what belongs in it is a real design decision.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Design a state schema for a given graph, deciding what fields belong in shared state versus what stays local to a node.

sections.title: 📋 What a state schema is
sections.content:
A typed definition (fields and their types) of everything that flows through the graph and that nodes can read and update — directly corresponding to the 'state' the Agents course's memory module discussed (the goal, accumulated history, scratchpad content), just now expressed as an explicit, checkable schema rather than an ad hoc dictionary.

```python
class AgentState(TypedDict):
    goal: str
    messages: list          # accumulated history
    scratchpad: list        # working notes, not shown to the user
    step_count: int         # control-flow flag a routing function checks
```

sections.title: 🎯 What typically belongs in state
sections.content:
- The **original task or goal**, so any node can access it without it being threaded through manually.
- The **accumulated history** of messages, tool calls, and observations — directly mapping onto the Agents course's short-term memory concept.
- Any **intermediate results** that later nodes will need, similar in spirit to a scratchpad.
- **Control-flow-relevant fields** — a step counter, a flag indicating whether a particular condition has been met — that routing functions will inspect.

sections.title: 🚫 What usually doesn't belong in state
sections.content: Purely local, temporary values a single node computes and uses immediately with no other node needing them — putting these in shared state adds noise without benefit and can make the state schema harder to reason about as the graph grows. Large raw data that's only needed transiently — better to process it down to what's actually needed before adding anything to state, mirroring the memory module's point that not everything needs to be retained.

sections.title: ✅ Why explicit schemas matter
sections.content: A typed schema catches a whole class of bugs (a node expecting a field to exist that another part of the graph never actually sets) before runtime, and makes it possible to inspect exactly what a graph's state looks like at any point during execution or in a checkpoint (the subject of the next module) — an explicit contract between nodes, rather than an implicit one that's only discoverable by reading every node's code.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Adding every value a node might conceivably need to the shared schema 'just in case.'** This directly contradicts the guidance in this lesson — a bloated schema with unused or rarely-used fields is harder to reason about, not more flexible.

**Storing large raw data (a full document, an entire search result set) in state instead of the processed result a later node actually needs.** This mirrors the same over-retention problem the memory module warned against — process data down before it enters shared state.

**Skipping type annotations on state fields to save a bit of upfront design time.** Doing this forfeits the exact bug-catching and inspectability benefits this lesson identifies as the whole point of an explicit schema.

questions.question: What does a LangGraph state schema define?
options: The visual layout of the graph diagram
A typed definition of everything that flows through the graph and that nodes can read and update
The specific LLM provider used by every node
The maximum number of nodes allowed in a graph
questions.explanation: The state schema is an explicit, typed contract for what data exists in the graph's shared state, which every node reads from and can update.

questions.question: What kind of value should generally NOT be added to shared graph state?
options: The original task or goal
A purely local, temporary value a single node computes and uses immediately with no other node needing it
A step counter used by a routing function
The accumulated history of messages and observations
questions.explanation: Values that stay entirely local to one node and aren't needed elsewhere add unnecessary noise to shared state without providing any benefit.

questions.question: What benefit does an explicit, typed state schema provide over an implicit, ad hoc state structure?
options: It makes the graph run without needing any nodes
It catches bugs where a node expects a field that's never actually set, and makes state inspectable at any point in execution
It eliminates the need for conditional edges
It automatically checkpoints the graph with no further configuration
questions.explanation: A typed schema acts as an explicit contract between nodes, catching mismatches early and enabling clear inspection of state at any point, unlike an implicit structure only discoverable by reading every node's code.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what four fields does AgentState define?
options: goal, messages, scratchpad, and step_count
prompt, model, parser, and chain
node, edge, state, and cycle
user_id, timestamp, topic, and query
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example defines AgentState as a TypedDict with exactly these four fields, matching what the lesson describes as typically belonging in state.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, which field is described as 'working notes, not shown to the user'?
options: scratchpad
goal
messages
step_count
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example comments the scratchpad field specifically as working notes not shown to the user, echoing the Agents course's scratchpad concept.

questions.question: Why does this lesson say large raw data that's only needed transiently shouldn't go directly into state?
options: Because it's better to process it down to what's actually needed before adding anything to state, mirroring the memory module's point that not everything needs to be retained
Because state schemas cannot technically hold large values under any circumstances
Because transient data is always automatically deleted regardless of where it's stored
Because large data always causes a graph to stop functioning entirely
questions.explanation: The lesson explicitly connects this to the earlier memory-module lesson's point about not retaining more than what's genuinely needed later.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against adding every value a node might conceivably need to the shared schema 'just in case'?
options: Because a bloated schema with unused or rarely-used fields is harder to reason about, not more flexible
Because LangGraph technically limits schemas to a fixed maximum number of fields
Because adding extra fields always breaks the graph's execution immediately
Because shared state cannot contain more than one field at a time
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is over-including fields preemptively, which directly undermines the clarity and reasoning benefits of a well-designed schema.

questions.question: Why does this lesson caution against skipping type annotations on state fields to save upfront design time?
options: Because doing this forfeits the exact bug-catching and inspectability benefits this lesson identifies as the whole point of an explicit schema
Because type annotations have no actual effect on how a graph behaves
Because skipping annotations always makes a graph run measurably faster
Because untyped fields are required for a graph to support conditional edges
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is skipping the very thing (explicit typing) that this lesson argues is what makes a schema catch bugs early and stay inspectable.

lessons.title: Reducers: How State Updates Actually Combine
lessons.description: When two nodes both want to update the same field, something has to decide how those updates combine — that's a reducer's job.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what a reducer does for a state field and give an example of when the default 'overwrite' behavior isn't what you want.

sections.title: 🔄 Default behavior: overwrite
sections.content: Without any special configuration, when a node returns an update to a state field, that update simply replaces the field's previous value. This is the right behavior for many fields — a status flag, a final answer field — where the newest value really should replace whatever was there before.

sections.title: ➕ When overwrite is wrong: accumulating lists
sections.content:
For a field like a message history or an accumulated list of observations, overwrite behavior is actively wrong — each node's update should be appended to what's already there, not replace it entirely (which would silently discard everything accumulated so far, including on every single loop iteration in a cyclic agent graph). A reducer function defines exactly how a new update combines with the existing value for that field — for a list-valued field, a common reducer simply concatenates the new items onto the existing list rather than replacing it.

```python
def append_reducer(existing: list, new: list) -> list:
    return existing + new

class AgentState(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list, append_reducer]   # accumulates every update
    final_answer: str                            # default overwrite is fine here
```

sections.title: 🧩 Reducers as part of the schema
sections.content: The reducer for a field is typically specified as part of the state schema definition itself, so it's an explicit, visible part of how that field behaves — anyone reading the schema can see not just what type a field holds, but how updates to it combine, rather than that behavior being an implicit assumption baked into node code that's easy to get wrong or forget.

sections.title: 🎯 Why this matters specifically for cyclic graphs
sections.content: In a graph with a loop (the reasoning-and-tool-execution cycle from the previous module, for instance), a message-history-style field gets updated on every single pass through the loop — if that field used overwrite semantics instead of an append-style reducer, each new loop iteration would erase the history from all previous iterations, breaking the model's ability to see what it already tried. Getting reducers right on the fields that accumulate across loop iterations is one of the most common early LangGraph mistakes to watch for.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Leaving an accumulating field on default overwrite semantics.** This is the single most common early LangGraph bug: a message-history or observation-list field silently loses everything from previous loop iterations instead of building up over time.

**Applying an append-style reducer to a field that should actually be replaced.** A status flag or a final-answer field generally wants the newest value, not a growing list of every value it's ever held — the right reducer depends on the field's actual semantics, not a one-size-fits-all default.

**Defining a reducer's logic separately from the schema instead of attaching it directly to the field.** Keeping the reducer visibly attached to the field it governs is what makes the update-combination behavior an explicit, readable part of the schema rather than an easy-to-miss implicit assumption.

questions.question: What is the default behavior when a node updates a state field with no reducer specified?
options: The update is appended to a list automatically
The update simply overwrites the field's previous value
The update is ignored entirely
The update triggers a checkpoint automatically
questions.explanation: Without a specific reducer, a state update replaces the field's prior value — appropriate for some fields but not for ones meant to accumulate over time.

questions.question: Why is default overwrite behavior wrong for a message-history-style field in a cyclic agent graph?
options: Overwrite behavior is never actually wrong for any field
Each loop iteration's update would erase the history from all previous iterations, breaking the agent's ability to see what it already tried
Message history fields cannot be represented in LangGraph state
Overwrite behavior only affects the graph's final node
questions.explanation: Since a cyclic graph updates accumulating fields on every pass through the loop, overwrite semantics would silently discard prior history each time, exactly the bug a proper append-style reducer prevents.

questions.question: Where is a field's reducer typically specified?
options: It cannot be specified anywhere — reducers don't exist in LangGraph
As part of the state schema definition itself, making it an explicit, visible part of the field's behavior
Only inside the routing function, never near the field definition
In a separate configuration file unrelated to the state schema
questions.explanation: Defining the reducer alongside the field in the schema makes the update-combination behavior explicit and visible to anyone reading the schema, rather than an implicit assumption.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what does append_reducer(existing, new) return?
options: existing + new, concatenating the new items onto the existing list
Only the new list, discarding existing entirely
Only the existing list, ignoring new entirely
An empty list regardless of the inputs
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example defines append_reducer to return existing + new, the concatenation that preserves prior history while adding the latest update.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, why does final_answer NOT use Annotated with a reducer?
options: Because the default overwrite behavior is fine for a field meant to hold just the newest value
Because string fields are technically incapable of having reducers
Because final_answer is never actually updated by any node
Because only list-typed fields are allowed to exist in a state schema
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example leaves final_answer on default overwrite semantics specifically because that field should hold the latest value, not accumulate a list of every value it's held.

questions.question: Why does this lesson describe getting reducers right as 'one of the most common early LangGraph mistakes to watch for'?
options: Because accumulating fields left on default overwrite silently lose history on every loop iteration, a bug that's easy to introduce and easy to miss
Because reducers are an obscure, rarely-used feature with little practical impact
Because LangGraph does not actually support custom reducers at all
Because this mistake only affects graphs with no cycles whatsoever
questions.explanation: The lesson explains this is common precisely because the default behavior silently does the wrong thing for accumulating fields, especially in the cyclic graphs central to agent loops.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against leaving an accumulating field on default overwrite semantics?
options: Because this is the single most common early LangGraph bug — the field silently loses everything from previous loop iterations instead of building up
Because overwrite semantics are always the correct choice for every field type
Because accumulating fields are incapable of ever being defined in a schema
Because this mistake only causes a minor, cosmetic issue with no functional impact
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is exactly the central point of the lesson: an accumulating field needs an append-style reducer, not the default overwrite.

questions.question: Why does this lesson caution against applying an append-style reducer to a field that should actually be replaced?
options: Because the right reducer depends on the field's actual semantics — a status flag or final-answer field generally wants the newest value, not a growing list
Because append-style reducers are technically incompatible with every field type
Because every field in a state schema must use the exact same reducer
Because applying the wrong reducer always causes the graph to crash immediately
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is a one-size-fits-all reducer choice, when different fields (accumulating history vs. a status flag) genuinely need different update-combination behavior.

lessons.title: Shared State vs. Per-Node Working Data
lessons.description: Not everything a node needs has to travel through the graph's shared state — knowing the difference keeps a graph's state schema clean.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Distinguish what belongs in a graph's shared state from what a node can compute and use locally without touching state at all.

sections.title: 🌐 Shared state: the graph's common ground
sections.content: Fields that multiple nodes need to read or that persist across loop iterations belong in shared state, following the schema design principles from earlier in this module — the goal, message history, control-flow flags, anything a routing function needs to inspect.

sections.title: 🧮 Per-node local computation
sections.content:
A node is still an ordinary function internally — it can do local computation, call helper functions, and use local variables that never touch the graph's state at all, exactly as in any other piece of code, as long as the final thing it returns to the graph is a proper state update. Not every intermediate value a node computes needs to become a state field just because the node happens to be part of a graph.

```python
def summarize_node(state):
    raw_docs = fetch_documents(state["query"])   # purely local, never touches state
    cleaned = [strip_boilerplate(d) for d in raw_docs]  # also local
    summary = llm.summarize(cleaned)
    return {"summary": summary}   # only the final result becomes a state update
```

sections.title: 🔌 Configuration and dependencies vs. state
sections.content: Things like which LLM client to use, API keys, or other configuration that doesn't change per-execution and isn't really part of the 'data flowing through the task' are typically handled separately from graph state (through configuration passed in when the graph is compiled or invoked), rather than being stuffed into the state schema alongside the actual task data — keeping the state schema focused on what it's actually for.

sections.title: 🎯 A practical guideline
sections.content: Ask, for any given piece of data: does more than one node need this, or does it need to survive across a loop iteration? If yes, it belongs in shared state. If it's purely internal to how one node does its job this one time, keep it local to that node's function and don't add it to the schema — this keeps the state schema focused on what actually needs to be shared, and easier for anyone to reason about as the graph grows.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Threading a node's purely internal intermediate values through the state schema.** The summarize_node example in this lesson shows raw_docs and cleaned staying local precisely because no other node needs them — pushing them into shared state anyway adds clutter with no payoff.

**Storing API keys or client configuration in the state schema alongside task data.** Configuration that doesn't vary per execution belongs in the graph's compile-time or invoke-time configuration, not mixed into the data that's actually flowing through the task.

**Skipping the 'does more than one node need this' check before adding a new state field.** This lesson's practical guideline exists specifically to catch fields that don't actually need to be shared before they clutter the schema.

questions.question: What kind of data belongs in a graph's shared state, according to this lesson?
options: Every single local variable any node ever computes
Data that multiple nodes need to read or that must persist across loop iterations
Only data related to the graph's visual diagram
API keys and client configuration
questions.explanation: Shared state is for data with a genuine cross-node or cross-iteration need — not every internal computation a node performs.

questions.question: Can a node use local variables and helper functions without putting everything into graph state?
options: No, every value computed inside a node must become a state field
Yes, a node is still an ordinary function internally and can use local computation as long as its final return is a proper state update
Only if the graph has no conditional edges
Local computation is not supported inside LangGraph nodes
questions.explanation: Nodes remain ordinary functions internally — local, node-specific computation doesn't need to be reflected in the graph's shared state schema.

questions.question: Where does configuration like API keys or which LLM client to use typically belong?
options: Directly inside the state schema alongside task data
Handled separately through configuration passed in when the graph is compiled or invoked, not stuffed into state
Hardcoded inside every node's function body with no central configuration
It cannot be configured at all in LangGraph
questions.explanation: Configuration that doesn't represent per-execution task data is kept separate from the state schema, keeping state focused on the data actually flowing through the task.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what does summarize_node ultimately return as its state update?
options: Only {"summary": summary}, not raw_docs or cleaned
The entire raw_docs list
Both raw_docs and cleaned, in addition to summary
Nothing — the function has no return value
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example shows only the final summary result being returned as the state update, while raw_docs and cleaned stay purely local to the function.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, why do raw_docs and cleaned never touch the graph's shared state?
options: Because they are purely local, intermediate values that no other node needs to see
Because LangGraph technically forbids local variables inside node functions
Because only string-typed values can ever be added to state
Because fetch_documents and strip_boilerplate are not real functions
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example specifically comments these variables as "purely local" and "also local", illustrating exactly the local-vs-shared distinction the lesson describes.

questions.question: What practical question does this lesson recommend asking to decide if a piece of data belongs in shared state?
options: Does more than one node need this, or does it need to survive across a loop iteration?
Is this data larger than 100 kilobytes?
Does this data include any numbers?
Was this data computed using an LLM call?
questions.explanation: The lesson's practical guideline is exactly this question — cross-node or cross-iteration need is the deciding factor, not the nature or size of the data itself.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against threading a node's purely internal intermediate values through the state schema?
options: Because the summarize_node example shows raw_docs and cleaned staying local precisely because no other node needs them — adding them to state adds clutter with no payoff
Because intermediate values are technically incapable of being stored anywhere
Because doing so always causes the graph to fail immediately
Because local variables cannot exist inside functions used as LangGraph nodes
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is exactly the anti-pattern its own code example avoids: pushing node-local values into shared state when nothing else in the graph needs them.

questions.question: Why does this lesson caution against storing API keys or client configuration in the state schema alongside task data?
options: Because configuration that doesn't vary per execution belongs in the graph's compile-time or invoke-time configuration, not mixed into the data actually flowing through the task
Because API keys cannot technically be represented as strings
Because state schemas are only allowed to contain numeric fields
Because mixing configuration into state always causes a security vulnerability
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is conflating configuration with task data, when the lesson explicitly recommends keeping them separate to preserve the state schema's focus and clarity.

lessons.title: Message-State Patterns for Conversational Graphs
lessons.description: Most agent and chatbot graphs converge on the same shape of state: an accumulating list of messages.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Describe the common message-list state pattern and why it's such a natural fit for conversational and tool-using graphs.

sections.title: 💬 Why messages as the core state shape
sections.content:
A conversational agent's entire relevant history — user turns, assistant responses, tool calls and their results — can be represented uniformly as a growing list of typed messages (user message, assistant message, tool message), which maps directly onto the chat-template and structured tool-calling formats covered in the LLM Engineering and Agents courses. Using this as the primary state field means the graph's history is already in the exact shape most chat model APIs expect, with minimal translation needed.

```python
class AgentState(TypedDict):
    messages: Annotated[list, add_messages]  # built-in append-style reducer

# a typical accumulated history:
# [HumanMessage("What's the weather in Tokyo?"),
#  AIMessage(tool_calls=[{"name": "get_weather", "args": {"city": "Tokyo"}}]),
#  ToolMessage(content="18°C, cloudy"),
#  AIMessage("It's 18°C and cloudy in Tokyo.")]
```

sections.title: ➕ The append reducer, applied here specifically
sections.content: This is the canonical example of the append-style reducer from earlier in this module: the messages field needs new messages added to the end of the existing list on every node update, never overwritten, since the whole point is preserving the full conversational and tool-use history across every loop iteration.

sections.title: 🏷️ Typed message roles
sections.content: Distinguishing message types (a user message, an assistant message, a tool result message) within the list — rather than one undifferentiated blob of text — lets nodes and routing functions inspect exactly what kind of thing just happened (did the last message request a tool call? was it a tool's result, or was it the assistant's final answer?), which is often exactly the condition a routing function needs to check to decide where to send control next.

sections.title: 🎯 Why this pattern is so common
sections.content: Because it maps so directly onto both how chat models are actually invoked (a list of messages) and onto the ReAct-style thought/action/observation history from the Agents course, most LangGraph tutorials and pre-built agent constructs default to this message-list pattern as the primary (sometimes the only) state field, with other fields added only when a specific graph genuinely needs additional data beyond the conversational history itself.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Storing conversation history as one big unstructured string instead of a typed message list.** This loses exactly the role information (user, assistant, tool) that routing functions and nodes need to inspect to make correct decisions.

**Forgetting to use an append-style reducer on the messages field.** This is the same reducer mistake from earlier in this module, applied to the single most common state field in LangGraph applications — an easy way to silently lose conversation history on every loop pass.

**Adding extra state fields for data that's already recoverable from the message list itself.** If the last tool result or the last user message is already sitting in the messages list, duplicating it into a separate field adds redundant state to keep in sync rather than just reading it from where it already lives.

questions.question: What is the core state shape used by most conversational and tool-using LangGraph agents?
options: A single unstructured string containing all history
An accumulating, append-only list of typed messages (user, assistant, tool)
A fixed-size array that gets overwritten each turn
A separate database table updated outside of graph state
questions.explanation: Representing history as a growing list of typed messages maps directly onto both chat model APIs and the thought/action/observation pattern from the Agents course.

questions.question: Why must the messages field use an append-style reducer rather than the default overwrite behavior?
options: Append-style reducers are required for all fields, not just messages
The whole point of the messages field is preserving full history across loop iterations, so new messages must be added rather than replacing what's there
Overwrite behavior would make the graph faster
Messages fields don't actually need any reducer at all
questions.explanation: This is a direct application of the earlier reducer lesson: since messages need to accumulate across every loop pass, an append reducer (not overwrite) is essential.

questions.question: Why is distinguishing typed message roles (user, assistant, tool) within the list useful?
options: It has no functional benefit, only cosmetic value
It lets nodes and routing functions inspect exactly what kind of thing just happened, which routing decisions often depend on
It prevents the list from ever growing beyond a fixed size
Typed roles are only relevant for training data, not runtime state
questions.explanation: Knowing whether the last message was a tool-call request, a tool result, or a final answer is often exactly the information a routing function needs to decide where control goes next.

questions.question: In this lesson's code example, what does add_messages do for the messages field?
options: Serves as the built-in append-style reducer, adding new messages to the existing list
Deletes the oldest message every time a new one is added
Converts every message into a single unstructured string
Removes the need for any typed message roles
questions.explanation: The lesson's code example annotates messages with add_messages specifically as its reducer, described as the built-in append-style reducer for accumulating message history.

questions.question: In this lesson's example message sequence, what type of message immediately follows the AIMessage with tool_calls?
options: A ToolMessage containing the tool's result
Another AIMessage with a different tool call
A HumanMessage starting a new conversation
Nothing — the sequence ends there
questions.explanation: The lesson's example sequence shows AIMessage(tool_calls=[...]) followed by ToolMessage(content="18°C, cloudy"), reflecting the request-then-result pattern typical of tool-using conversations.

questions.question: Why does this lesson say the message-list pattern requires 'minimal translation' for most chat model APIs?
options: Because the graph's history is already in the exact shape (a list of messages) most chat model APIs expect
Because chat model APIs never actually accept a list of messages as input
Because translation is always required no matter what state shape is used
Because message-list state is incompatible with tool calls
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that representing history as a message list mirrors how chat models are actually invoked, minimizing the conversion work needed between graph state and model input.

questions.question: Why does this lesson warn against storing conversation history as one big unstructured string instead of a typed message list?
options: Because this loses exactly the role information (user, assistant, tool) that routing functions and nodes need to inspect to make correct decisions
Because unstructured strings are technically incapable of being stored in state at all
Because typed message lists always use less memory than a single string
Because a single string is required for a graph to support any conditional edges
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is losing the structured role information that a typed message list preserves, which routing logic often depends on.

questions.question: Why does this lesson caution against adding extra state fields for data that's already recoverable from the message list itself?
options: Because duplicating data that's already in the messages list adds redundant state to keep in sync rather than just reading it from where it already lives
Because the message list is technically incapable of holding tool results
Because extra state fields are always forbidden by LangGraph's schema rules
Because reading from the message list is always slower than a dedicated field
questions.explanation: The lesson's stated common mistake is unnecessary duplication — introducing a separate field for information the messages list already captures, creating an extra thing to keep consistent for no real benefit.
